official_title: Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026. If enacted, this Initiative would: (a) Prohibit any person from force-feeding a bird for the purpose of enlarging the bird's liver beyond normal size; (b) Ban the sale or distribution of any product resulting from force-feeding a bird, including foie gras; (c) Define force-feeding as inserting a tube into the bird's throat to deliver excessive feed; (d) Provide for enforcement by the Department of Energy and Environment during routine food safety inspections; and (e) Provide for civil penalties.
plain_summary: Bans force-feeding birds to fatten their livers, and bans restaurants and stores in DC from selling, serving or distributing foie gras and other fattened-liver products (pates, spreads, processed meats). The Department of Energy and Environment would enforce it through food safety inspections and a public complaint process. Fines run $1,000 to $5,000 per violation, with each day counted separately; repeat violators within 12 months can lose their business license. It does not ban eating foie gras you bought elsewhere. It takes effect July 1, 2027.
yes_means: DC restaurants and stores can no longer sell, serve or distribute foie gras or other fattened bird liver products, starting July 1, 2027.
no_means: Nothing changes; foie gras stays legal to sell and serve in DC.
current_law: DC has no law on force-feeding birds or on the sale of foie gras. No foie gras is produced in DC; the measure's farm ban would apply to future operations. California and New York City have passed similar bans; Denver voters face a parallel initiative on November 3, 2026.
fiscal_impact: No official fiscal impact statement was located this run. The measure says its applicability date (July 1, 2027) can slide if its fiscal effect must first be included in an approved budget. The enforcement agency (DOEE) would take on inspections, a complaint process and a quarterly public violations database.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot summary says force-feeding means 'inserting a tube into the bird's throat,' but the full text defines it more broadly as any process that makes a bird eat more than it would on its own. The ballot title reads like an animal-welfare question; the practical effect in DC is a ban on selling and serving foie gras, since no birds are raised for it here. 'Yes, to approve' enacts the ban. 'No, to reject' keeps foie gras legal. The measure is the LAST item on the ballot, after your ANC race, and easy to miss. Like all DC initiatives, it goes through a 30-day congressional review after passage, and the Council can later amend it.

supporters_case.text: Pro-Animal DC, which gathered more than 46,000 signatures (about twice the 23,940 required), says force-feeding is cruel and that 'just because it's a niche product doesn't mean that we should accept this form of animal cruelty.' It cites a poll finding 78% of DC voters support a ban and points to similar bans in California and New York City.

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition campaign has formed. Chef Bart Hutchins of Butterworth's, the most vocal opponent, says the two U.S. foie gras farms have 'incredibly high standards,' that singling out foie gras while ignoring factory-farmed pork and chicken is inconsistent, and that 'I'm not going to bend to these people.' Columnist Marc Fisher (City Cast DC) calls it 'an absurd attempt to mandate what people may eat.' Another chef asked, 'Who's going to do the enforcement, by the way?'
